title: Aging‐Induced Ductile‐Brittle‐Ductile Transition in High‐Entropy Alloys and its Implications

questions.broad: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.
questions.problem_constrained: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.
questions.expert_context: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.
